summary: Henry Island lighttower off Port Hood, Cape Breton: lit 1 December 1902, automated 1960s, the island privately owned since 1992, the Coast Guard still maintains the light.

lens.note: Fourth-order dioptric installed 1966 (NSLPS). The 1902 light was catoptric (Department report for fiscal 1902).

structures.note: Octagonal wooden tower of plank on plank construction with a cast-iron lantern. Coast Guard list gives 11.6 m; the 1902 report gives 53 ft to the vane; NSLPS gives a tower height of 38 ft.
Wooden keeper's dwelling, painted white, 165 ft south of the tower (1902 report). Restored (NSLPS).

staffing.note: Illuminant changed to acetylene so the light could be automated, during the last keeper's term (LF). The local history gives 13 June 1962. NSLPS lists automated by 1993.

access.note: Privately owned island, reached by boat only. Trips by appointment, weather permitting (NSLPS).

events.note: Octagonal wooden tower with a red iron lantern; contract to Jos. McDonald for $3,489 (report for fiscal 1902). NSLPS names the engineer as Joseph MacDonald at the same cost. Heritage statement: design by the Engineering Branch.
Put in operation 1 December 1902 (report for fiscal 1903).
Illuminant changed to acetylene so the light could be automated (LF). Local history: automated 13 June 1962. NSLPS: automated by 1993 (conflict).
Electrified (NSLPS). Solar panel fixed to the gallery railing to charge batteries feeding a new beacon in the lantern (LF).
Recognized federal heritage building; statement numbered 90-290 (register). LF gives 1991.
Island privately owned since 1992 (NSLPS; local history).
Placed second in the Ebb Tide category of the Nova Scotia crowdfunding contest This Lighthouse Matters; the $20,000 prize paid for re-shingling and staining the tower (LF).

corrections.why: The register's statement names the Canadian Coast Guard as custodian and NSLPS says the light is still maintained by it. The island is privately owned, which stays in the ownership field. Reviewed by a human, not applied.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Department's 1903 index calls the Henry Island light a new light. A Port Hood local history calls the 1902 tower the second lighthouse on the island. No source read names an earlier light, so the story gives both and does not decide.
Lighthouse Friends names Stanley Morrison (1961 to 1962) as the last keeper. The Port Hood local history names Charlie MacLennan. Both are in the story.

Lighthouse Friends ties the acetylene change to Stanley Morrison's time (1961 to 1962). The local history gives 13 June 1962. NSLPS lists automated by 1993, which is a 'by' date in its list and not an event date.

The 1902 report gives 240 ft above high water; the current Coast Guard list gives a focal height of 61.0 m (about 200 ft); NSLPS gives 200 ft. The story gives the 1902 figure as the report's and the current figure as the Coast Guard's.
The 1902 report says visible 22 miles, without naming the unit. The Coast Guard list's nominal range is 9 nautical miles. The story gives the report's words only.
The 1902 report gives 53 ft to the vane; NSLPS gives a tower height of 38 ft; the Coast Guard list gives 11.6 m (38 ft) for the structure. The story gives all three with their sources.
Lighthouse Friends dates the federal heritage recognition to 1991. The statement is numbered 90-290. The story gives Lighthouse Friends' date and the statement number.

notes_for_editor: Thin on events: no storm, wreck or rescue for Henry Island appears in the Marine reports for 1900 to 1924 (grep returned only station and light lists), so the story has no storms chapter. The keeper 'McLennan, John Angus' was matched by position in the 1904 list (scan 175, printed p. 162) and checked on the page image on 2026-10-27: July 21, 1903, 400.00. The 1903 list (scan 232, printed p. 219, the same page as the Flint Island McKenzie row in the Flint story) also shows him, with 405.00 printed; the story uses the $400 from Lighthouse Friends. The NSLPS tower height is 38 ft; an earlier 56 ft figure in this record was an error. The contract's 'Jos. McDonald' (report) and 'Joseph MacDonald' (NSLPS, local history) are assumed to be the same man; the story says the sources name him differently. The owner is a private individual who has a public profile; the story says only that the island is privately owned since 1992, and does not name the owner. Lighthouse Friends cites a 2004 Globe and Mail article, which was not read (not accessible here). The local history listing is a community site, so the 'believed' naming and the 'second lighthouse' claim are reported with attribution. Chronicling America was not searched for this station. Lighthouse Friends photographs and the NSLPS photograph are not mirrored.
